text:
Rivers are the planet's great connectors, moving water, sediment and life from high ground to the sea. A river usually starts as a spring, a melting glacier, or rain gathering in the hills. Small streams join as it goes downhill, and each one adds volume until the channel can carve valleys, cut canyons and wear mountains down one grain at a time.

People have always settled beside rivers. Mesopotamia grew up between the Tigris and the Euphrates, Egypt along the Nile, and early Indian and Chinese cities along the Indus and the Yellow River. Rivers gave these societies drinking water, fertile floodplains, fish and easy trade routes. Floods destroyed homes, but they also left behind the rich silt that fed whole nations.

Ecologically, rivers carry a lot of life. Salmon swim upstream to spawn, and their bodies feed forests far from the ocean. Wetlands along the banks filter pollutants, shelter birds and soak up floodwater. Deltas, where rivers fan out into the sea, are among the most productive habitats on Earth.

Today rivers are under pressure from dams, pollution, overuse and climate change. Some no longer reach the ocean at all. Restoring them by removing old dams, cleaning up runoff and protecting watersheds is one of the most hopeful kinds of environmental work.
